title: Reviewing Risky Git Commands
subtopics: Checking repository state before destructive actions
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and boundaries of reviewing risky git commands.
Choose and interpret a Git command relevant to reviewing risky git commands using a disposable repository.
Verify the result with repository state or history and identify one safety limitation.

content.intro: This lesson introduces reviewing risky git commands as part of Git Security and Professional Best Practices. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: Git stores and transfers source history but does not automatically make that history private or remove leaked secrets. Security depends on identity, repository permissions, review, signatures, and incident response.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Git stores and transfers source history but does not automatically make that history private or remove leaked secrets. Security depends on identity, repository permissions, review, signatures, and incident response.

For **Reviewing Risky Git Commands**, keep the named subtopics in view: Force pushing; Hard resets and cleaning; History rewriting; Checking repository state before destructive actions. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Use the preview first and never add force or ignored-file flags without reviewing the exact target in a disposable repository.

content_blocks.expected_output: A dry-run list of untracked paths that a clean command would remove; no files are deleted by this preview.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use the preview first and never add force or ignored-file flags without reviewing the exact target in a disposable repository.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a disposable repository. If the exercise changes state, check git status and git log before and after; discard the practice directory only after confirming it contains no valuable work.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf web lesson page does not execute arbitrary Git commands. Run commands locally in a disposable repository with a Git version appropriate to your task. Placeholder paths, branches, commit IDs and repository URLs must be replaced with values from that practice repository.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

task: Using a repository you own or are authorized to access, record the remote URLs, fetch or inspect remote history, compare it with the local branch, and document what would change before pushing or opening a review.
hints: Use a read-only inspection command before any operation that changes files, refs or remote state.
After the example, verify with git status --short --branch and/or git log --oneline --graph as appropriate.
expected_output: A dry-run list of untracked paths that a clean command would remove; no files are deleted by this preview.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.

summary: Reviewing Risky Git Commands is covered through these syllabus topics: Force pushing; Hard resets and cleaning; History rewriting; Checking repository state before destructive actions.
Choose the command for the intended effect; understand whether it changes files, the index, local references, or remote state.
Verify the result, record unexpected output, and retain a recovery path for risky operations.
